findings.how_to_check: Search CODE/ for profile validation code: Select-String -Path "CODE\*.do" -Pattern "transcription_accuracy|profile". Check DHTS-2024-11-18.tex lines 70, 104-106, and lines 633-643 to confirm that the table has bracketed placeholders [X]-[W] and is marked forthcoming.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove or qualify the empirical claims in the Abstract and Introduction until the FamilySearch profile validation is computed and the table populated. In the interim, cite the middle-initial validation and cross-algorithm robustness results as the evidence for match quality.
findings.title: Independent genealogical profile validation is claimed as an empirical result in the Abstract and Introduction but is unimplemented in code and marked forthcoming in text
findings.what_the_code_does: The Abstract (lines 70-71) states that validation against independent genealogical records confirms genuine accuracy gains, and the Introduction (lines 104-106) states that machine learning transcriptions achieve higher match rates against FamilySearch.org profile names than Ancestry or FamilySearch census transcriptions for discordant records. However, in Section 4.2 (lines 633-643), the table comparing transcription sources to profile names is commented out with unfilled placeholders ([X]%, [Y]%, [Z]%, [W]%), line 643 explicitly states that results are forthcoming, and no script in CODE/ executes this validation on the 1% sample.
findings.why_it_matters: Presenting a forthcoming validation analysis with placeholder numbers as an established empirical result in the Abstract and Introduction is a direct claims-vs-code contradiction that referees will immediately flag.

Tabulate the merge attrition in CODE/create_figures_SSHA2025.do:61-87 to inspect the 29,344 omitted records.

If the headline linkage table requires successful merge into socio-demographic or link files, document the attrition rule and update the sample counts in Section 3.1 and Table 3 note accordingly.
findings.title: The headline linkage table silently uses smaller record counts than the analysis sample defined in the text
findings.what_the_code_does: In CODE/munir_figures_for_nber.do:324-345, the analysis sample is established as 51,066,203 records (males aged 10+ with all four names present), including 14,427,780 discordant target records; these exact counts are cited in DHTS-2024-11-18.tex:383-386 and appear in Table 1 (balance_allstates.tex) and Table 2 (incongruent_allstates.tex). However, CODE/create_figures_SSHA2025.do:61-87 produces Table 3 (avg_performance_allstates.tex) by merging census1940_all_labeled_data.dta with all_states_socio_demo_char_for_SSHA2025.dta and two link files (keep(1 3)), then filtering keep if sex==1 & age>=10, resulting in 51,036,859 all records and 14,416,543 target records.
findings.why_it_matters: A silent discrepancy of 29,344 records in the overall sample and 11,237 records in the target sample exists between Section 3.1 / Tables 1-2 and the headline results in Table 3. Despite LaTeX comments at line 513 noting that manual entry previously caused this table to drift out of step with the balance tables, Table 3 still does not match the analysis sample Ns.

findings.how_to_check: Inspect CODE/compute_model_agreement_on_discordant.do:119-124 to confirm that the script only tests string equality between sources without image review or external ground truth. Contrast with DHTS-2024-11-18.tex:293-294.
findings.suggested_fix: State descriptively that the model agrees more often with FamilySearch than Ancestry among discordant records. Remove the claim that this indicates FamilySearch transcriptions are more reliable on average unless supported by an image-adjudicated ground truth sample.
findings.title: Model agreement with FamilySearch is interpreted as evidence of FamilySearch transcription reliability without ground truth
findings.what_the_code_does: In CODE/compute_model_agreement_on_discordant.do:119-124, the code counts exact string equality between the model and FamilySearch (51.8%) versus Ancestry (14.3%) among discordant records. DHTS-2024-11-18.tex:293-294 asserts that this split suggests 'FamilySearch transcriptions may be somewhat more reliable on average.'
findings.why_it_matters: Neither Ancestry nor FamilySearch is ground truth. A higher rate of agreement indicates that the model's output resembles FamilySearch's transcription more often, which can result from model training distributions, preprocessing, or shared ditto resolution rules rather than higher transcription accuracy. Conflating agreement with reliability violates the core domain distinction of the project.

findings.title: Legibility quartile statistics in Section 4.3 are carried over from Rhode Island exploratory code rather than all-states analysis
findings.what_the_code_does: DHTS-2024-11-18.tex:709-711 claims that enumeration districts in the lowest quartile of legibility show '125% higher rates of transcription disagreement and 30% lower baseline linking rates.' In CODE/munir_figures_for_nber.do:566-692, these quartile comparisons were calculated in an exploratory block restricted to Rhode Island (merging rhode_island_socio_demo_char.dta). No national 49-jurisdiction script computes these figures.
findings.why_it_matters: The paper claims to report all results on a 49-jurisdiction national sample, but quotes specific percentages computed only on the Rhode Island pilot sample.

findings.how_to_check: Review DHTS-2024-11-18.tex:179-180, 258-276, and 870-892. Search CODE/ for any script evaluating out-of-sample sequence/token accuracy.
findings.suggested_fix: Label the test set metrics in Table 1 as 'Agreement with Consensus Commercial Transcriptions' rather than 'Accuracy', reserving accuracy for evaluations against independent genealogical records or hand-adjudicated samples.
findings.title: Test set sequence and token accuracy metrics evaluate consensus commercial agreement, not adjudicated ground truth
findings.what_the_code_does: Table 1 (lines 258-270) and Appendix A.4 report 97.38% first name and 94.54% last name 'Sequence Accuracy', evaluated on a test set restricted to records where Ancestry and FamilySearch agree. The repository contains no evaluation script or adjudicated truth dataset.
findings.why_it_matters: Measuring exact match against consensus commercial transcriptions identifies agreement on easy records, not ground truth accuracy. Consensus labels can share systematic errors. Presenting agreement as accuracy overstates the evaluation's benchmark.

review_limits: The underlying census, transcription, image, linkage, and Stata datasets are stored on external paths (D:\Dropbox, F:\) and were unavailable, so runtime execution and recomputation of empirical estimates could not be performed.

The repository contains no machine learning model training or inference scripts (only Stata analysis code and utility image scripts), so model architecture details, training procedures, and sequence/token accuracy test evaluations could not be reproduced from source.

The external Deaglan Jakob linkage package (F:\Deaglan\Census_Transcriptions\) is outside this repository; its results were reviewed via the committed table exhibits, PROVENANCE.md, and their quotation in the paper.
structured_output.summary: The paper makes strong empirical claims that exceed the code's backing: external genealogical profile validation is claimed in the Abstract and Introduction despite being unimplemented in code and marked forthcoming in the text, and higher model agreement with FamilySearch is treated as evidence of FamilySearch reliability without ground truth. In addition, the headline results table silently drops 29,344 records relative to the declared analysis sample, and several text descriptions describe obsolete Rhode Island-era figure layouts and quartile statistics. The single most important fix before submission is to align the claims in the Abstract and Introduction with the implemented analyses and reconcile the sample denominators across the exhibits.

summary.description: Two to four sentences. The overall state of the reviewed work and the single most important thing to fix. No preamble.

dimensions_reviewed.description: Which scope dimensions were actually reviewed in this run.

findings.description: Defects and concerns, ordered most severe first. Empty if none. Do not pad with stylistic observations.

severity.description: blocker: a reported result is wrong. major: a referee would demand it. minor: real but survivable. nit: cosmetic.

confidence.description: verified: traced in the source. likely: strongly implied but depends on unseen data. speculative: a question, not an established defect.

title.description: One line, stating the defect itself, not its category.

location.description: path:line, or path:line-line. Several may be comma-separated. Required: a finding without a location is not a finding.

what_the_code_does.description: Precisely what the code computes, quoting the relevant expression. Contrast with what it was evidently intended to compute.

why_it_matters.description: The consequence for a number or claim in the paper. If there is no consequence, the severity is nit.

how_to_check.description: A concrete command, tabulation, or count the author can run to confirm or refute this in minutes.

suggested_fix.description: The change, specific enough to act on. Do not apply it yourself.

verified_clean.description: Things explicitly checked that were fine. This is what makes a short findings list trustworthy rather than lazy.

evidence.description: How it was confirmed, with path:line where applicable.

review_limits.description: What this review could NOT establish: data not readable, pipeline not runnable, paper text unavailable, Stata semantics not verifiable by reading. Be explicit; silence here reads as false assurance.
